title: R and Python Together: Palmer Penguins
text:
This post demonstrates how R and Python can be used together in a single Quarto document. R is used to calculate the mean body mass of each penguin species. The resulting R object is then passed to Python, where it is used for an additional calculation.
The data come from the Palmer Penguins dataset from Palmer Station Antarctica LTER.

title: R and Python Together: Palmer Penguins
text:
This post demonstrates how R and Python can be used together in a single Quarto document. R is used to calculate the mean body mass of each penguin species. The resulting R object is then passed to Python, where it is used for an additional calculation.
The data come from the Palmer Penguins dataset from Palmer Station Antarctica LTER.

title: R and Python Together: Palmer Penguins
text:
R: Calculate Mean Body Mass
First, R loads the Palmer Penguins data and calculates the mean body mass for each species.

library(palmerpenguins)
library(dplyr)
library(reticulate)

penguin_summary <- penguins |>
  filter(!is.na(body_mass_g)) |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(
    mean_body_mass_g = mean(body_mass_g),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

penguin_summary

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  species   mean_body_mass_g
  <fct>                <dbl>
1 Adelie               3701.
2 Chinstrap            3733.
3 Gentoo               5076.


The object penguin_summary was created in R. It contains one row for each penguin species and its mean body mass.

title: R and Python Together: Palmer Penguins
text:
Python: Receive the R Object
The following Python chunk accesses the object created in R through r.penguin_summary.

penguin_summary_python = r.penguin_summary

penguin_summary_python

     species  mean_body_mass_g
0     Adelie       3700.662252
1  Chinstrap       3733.088235
2     Gentoo       5076.016260


Python is therefore using the result produced by R rather than loading the original dataset and repeating the analysis.

title: R and Python Together: Palmer Penguins
text:
Python: Use the Transferred Object
Next, Python uses the transferred object to determine which species has the highest mean body mass.

heaviest_species = penguin_summary_python.loc[
    penguin_summary_python["mean_body_mass_g"].idxmax()
]

heaviest_species

species                 Gentoo
mean_body_mass_g    5076.01626
Name: 2, dtype: object


The result identifies the penguin species with the highest average body mass based on the summary originally calculated in R.

title: R and Python Together: Palmer Penguins
text:
Conclusion
This post demonstrates how R and Python can work together in one Quarto document. R loaded and summarized the Palmer Penguins data and created the penguin_summary object. Python then received that R object and used it for an additional calculation.
This demonstrates that an object computed in one language can be passed to and used by another language within the same reproducible Quarto document.

section: My First Week of MDS: A New Chapter Begins
text:
My First Week of MDS: A New Chapter Begins
There are some moments in life that feel both exciting and overwhelming at the same time. Starting my MDS was one of those moments.
My first week of MDS has been a mix of new experiences, new people, unfamiliar routines, and a lot of thoughts about what lies ahead. After working toward this next step for so long, actually being here feels a little surreal.

title: My first weeks in MDS
text:
The First Day
Walking into university on the first day, I had so many emotions running through my mind. I was excited to begin this new chapter, but I was also nervous. Everything felt new—the surroundings, the people, the classrooms, and even the feeling of being a postgraduate student.
There was also a quiet realization that this wasn’t just another academic milestone. MDS is a serious commitment, and I knew that the next few years would challenge me in ways I hadn’t experienced before.

title: My first weeks in MDS
text:
Meeting New People
One of the best parts of the first week was meeting my batchmates and getting to know the people I’ll be spending the next few years with.
At first, everyone seemed a little reserved and unsure, probably because we were all trying to find our place. Slowly, conversations started happening, introductions turned into jokes, and unfamiliar faces began to feel a little more familiar.
It’s comforting to realize that everyone is experiencing some version of the same nervousness and excitement.

title: My first weeks in MDS
text:
Getting Used to the Routine
The first week also meant trying to understand a completely new routine.
There was a lot to take in—classes, departments, faculty, clinical responsibilities, schedules, and countless little things that you don’t really think about until you’re actually there.
I’m slowly learning that MDS isn’t just about studying harder. It’s also about managing time, staying organized, being responsible, and learning how to balance academics with everything else.

title: My first weeks in MDS
text:
The Reality of MDS
Perhaps the biggest realization of my first week is that MDS is going to push me out of my comfort zone.
There will be days when everything goes well and days when I question whether I can keep up. There will be new skills to learn, mistakes to make, difficult cases to understand

title: Exploring the Palmer Penguins Dataset
text:
The Palmer Penguins dataset contains measurements collected from three penguin species in the Palmer Archipelago, Antarctica: Adelie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo. It includes several physical measurements for individual penguins, such as body mass, flipper length, bill length, and bill depth, as well as information about species, sex, island, and year.
In this post, I use R to explore two questions:

How does body mass differ among the three penguin species?
What is the relationship between flipper length and body mass?

The analysis includes basic data exploration, handling of missing values, numerical summaries, and visualizations.

text:
The Palmer Penguins dataset contains measurements collected from three penguin species in the Palmer Archipelago, Antarctica: Adelie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo. It includes several physical measurements for individual penguins, such as body mass, flipper length, bill length, and bill depth, as well as information about species, sex, island, and year.
In this post, I use R to explore two questions:

How does body mass differ among the three penguin species?
What is the relationship between flipper length and body mass?

The analysis includes basic data exploration, handling of missing values, numerical summaries, and visualizations.

title: Exploring the Palmer Penguins Dataset
text:
Loading the packages
First, I load the packages required for the analysis.

library(palmerpenguins)
library(tidyverse)

title: Exploring the Palmer Penguins Dataset
text:
Data
The data used in this analysis come from the Palmer Penguins dataset from Palmer Station Antarctica LTER.
The palmerpenguins package provides the dataset, while functions from the tidyverse are used for data manipulation and visualization.

title: Exploring the Palmer Penguins Dataset
text:
Exploring the data
Before beginning the analysis, I inspect the first few rows of the dataset.

head(penguins)

# A tibble: 6 × 8
  species island    bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_mm body_mass_g
  <fct>   <fct>              <dbl>         <dbl>             <int>       <int>
1 Adelie  Torgersen           39.1          18.7               181        3750
2 Adelie  Torgersen           39.5          17.4               186        3800
3 Adelie  Torgersen           40.3          18                 195        3250
4 Adelie  Torgersen           NA            NA                  NA          NA

6 Adelie  Torgersen           39.3          20.6               190        3650
# ℹ 2 more variables: sex <fct>, year <int>


I also examine the dimensions of the dataset.

dim(penguins)

[1] 344   8


Each row represents an individual penguin, while the columns represent different variables measured or recorded for that penguin.
The variables that are particularly important for this analysis are:

species: penguin species
body_mass_g: body mass measured in grams
flipper_length_mm: flipper length measured in millimetres

title: Exploring the Palmer Penguins Dataset
text:
Handling missing values
Before creating the summaries and visualizations, I check for missing values in the two numerical variables used in this analysis.

penguins |>
  summarise(
    missing_body_mass = sum(is.na(body_mass_g)),
    missing_flipper_length = sum(is.na(flipper_length_mm))
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  missing_body_mass missing_flipper_length
              <int>                  <int>
1                 2                      2


Because the analysis depends on both body mass and flipper length, I create a cleaned dataset containing only observations for which both measurements are available.

penguins_clean <- penguins |>
  drop_na(body_mass_g, flipper_length_mm)

I can compare the number of observations before and after cleaning.

nrow(penguins)

[1] 344

nrow(penguins_clean)

[1] 342


Removing these incomplete observations allows the same cleaned dataset to be used consistently throughout the analysis.

title: Exploring the Palmer Penguins Dataset
section: Question 1: How does body mass differ among penguin species?
text:
Question 1: How does body mass differ among penguin species?
The first question examines how body mass differs among the three penguin species.
I begin by calculating several summary statistics for each species.

body_mass_summary <- penguins_clean |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_body_mass = mean(body_mass_g),
    median_body_mass = median(body_mass_g),
    sd_body_mass = sd(body_mass_g),
    min_body_mass = min(body_mass_g),
    max_body_mass = max(body_mass_g)
  )

body_mass_summary

# A tibble: 3 × 7
  species       n mean_body_mass median_body_mass sd_body_mass min_body_mass
  <fct>     <int>          <dbl>            <dbl>        <dbl>         <int>
1 Adelie      151          3701.             3700         459.          2850
2 Chinstrap    68          3733.             3700         384.          2700
3 Gentoo      123          5076.             5000         504.          3950
# ℹ 1 more variable: max_body_mass <int>


The mean and median describe the typical body mass for each species. The standard deviation describes how much body mass varies within each species, while the minimum and maximum show the observed range.

Visualizing body mass by species
A boxplot provides another way to compare the body-mass distributions of the three species.

ggplot(
  penguins_clean,
  aes(
    x = species,
    y = body_mass_g,
    fill = species
  )
) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Body Mass of Palmer Penguins by Species",
    x = "Species",
    y = "Body Mass (g)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  guides(fill = "none")










Interpretation
The numerical summaries and boxplot show clear differences in body mass among the three species. Gentoo penguins tend to have greater body masses than Adelie and Chinstrap penguins. Adelie and Chinstrap penguins have more similar body-mass distributions, although body mass still varies within each species.
The summary statistics provide numerical information about the centre, variability, and range of body mass, while the boxplot makes it easier to visually compare the distributions across species.

title: Exploring the Palmer Penguins Dataset
section: Question 2: What is the relationship between flipper length and body mass?
text:
Question 2: What is the relationship between flipper length and body mass?
The second question investigates whether penguins with longer flippers also tend to have greater body mass.
First, I calculate the overall correlation between the two numerical variables.

penguins_clean |>
  summarise(
    correlation = cor(flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g)
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 1
  correlation
        <dbl>
1       0.871


The correlation provides a numerical measure of the direction and strength of the relationship between flipper length and body mass.
I also calculate the correlation separately for each species.

penguins_clean |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(
    correlation = cor(flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g)
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  species   correlation
  <fct>           <dbl>
1 Adelie          0.468
2 Chinstrap       0.642
3 Gentoo          0.703


Calculating the correlation separately for each species helps determine whether the relationship between flipper length and body mass is also present within individual species, rather than being driven only by differences among species.

Visualizing the relationship
Because both variables are numerical, a scatterplot is useful for examining their relationship.

ggplot(
  penguins_clean,
  aes(
    x = flipper_length_mm,
    y = body_mass_g,
    color = species
  )
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "Relationship Between Flipper Length and Body Mass",
    subtitle = "Palmer Penguins",
    x = "Flipper Length (mm)",
    y = "Body Mass (g)",
    color = "Species"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()










Interpretation
The scatterplot shows a positive relationship between flipper length and body mass. In general, penguins with longer flippers also tend to have greater body mass.
The species groups are also visible in the plot. Gentoo penguins generally appear toward the upper-right portion of the graph, corresponding to longer flippers and greater body mass. Adelie and Chinstrap penguins tend to have shorter flippers and lower body masses.
The species-specific correlations provide additional information about the relationship within each species. Comparing these values with the overall correlation helps distinguish the within-species relationships from the overall pattern observed when all three species are considered together.

title: Exploring the Palmer Penguins Dataset
text:
Conclusion
This analysis used the Palmer Penguins dataset to investigate differences in body mass among species and the relationship between flipper length and body mass.
Before conducting the analysis, observations with missing body-mass or flipper-length measurements were removed so that the same cleaned dataset could be used consistently throughout the post.
For the first question, the numerical summaries and boxplot showed that body mass differs across species, with Gentoo penguins generally having greater body mass than Adelie and Chinstrap penguins. The summary statistics also provided information about the centre, variability, and range of body mass within each species.
For the second question, the overall correlation and scatterplot indicated a positive relationship between flipper length and body mass. Penguins with longer flippers generally tended to be heavier. Calculating the correlation separately for each species also allowed this relationship to be examined within each species rather than only across the complete dataset.

title: About ME
text:
I am a Master of Data Science student at the University of British Columbia with a background in Applied Mathematics and experience in statistics, programming, and quantitative analysis.
My academic background includes research in biomathematics, where I worked on mathematical models to study biological systems and explored how quantitative methods can be used to understand complex real-world processes. This experience strengthened my interest in modelling, data analysis, and research-driven problem solving.
I also participated in AI4Good, where I worked on an applied machine learning project focused on developing an assistive image-classification system. That experience gave me hands-on exposure to the challenges of working with real-world data, model development, evaluation, and communicating the limitations and practical impact of AI systems.
Through the MDS program, I am continuing to strengthen my skills in Python, R, machine learning, statistical modelling, data visualization, and data communication. My goal is to build a career in data science where I can combine my mathematical background, research experience, and interest in machine learning to solve meaningful problems.
